title: Beyond Generative LLMs: Architecting High-Speed Decision Gates with TypeSafe AI's Jev
description: A deep architectural dive into decision models versus generative text models. Learn how TypeSafe AI's Jev delivers sub-100ms deterministic routing, inline agent guardrails, and cost-optimized LLM pipelines.
text: In modern AI engineering, teams frequently fall into a costly anti-pattern: using multi-billion-parameter autoregressive models for simple classification, routing, and verification tasks. When an incoming customer ticket needs triage, a user prompt requires security filtering, or an autonomous browser agent must select the next button to click, invoking a generative model like GPT-4o or Claude 3.7 introduces: Multi-second latency waiting for token generation. Parsing overhead with fragile JSON output schemas. Runaway API costs burning token budgets on binary yes/no decisions. Enter TypeSafe AI's Jev —a specialized decision model engineered not to generate paragraphs of text, but to evaluate typed, deterministic questions directly over state in sub-second latency. In this article, we explore how decision models fundamentally differ from text generators, analyze six production use cases, and implement an end-to-end hybrid triage gate in Python. 1. Paradigm Shift: Text Generation vs. Deterministic Verdicts Traditional LLMs predict the next token in a sequence. To make a decision, an LLM must generate text tokens that your application then deserializes and validates: [Prompt + Context] ──► [Autoregressive Generation] ──► "```json\n{"action": ...}\n```" ──► Pydantic Parse In contrast, Jev takes an arbitrary state payload (raw text, structured JSON, code, or DOM nodes) and evaluates a battery of strictly typed questions in a single forward pass: ┌── Question 1 (choice) ──► Selected Option [State / Context] ──►│── Question 2 (noul) ──► Boolean Flag (True/False + Prob) └── Question 3 (score) ──► Continuous Metric (0 - 100) The Three Typed Primitives of Jev Instead of freeform prompts, Jev operates on three mathematical primitives: choice : Selects exactly one label from a predefined list of string categories (e.g., routing queues, model tiers, tool actions). noul : A probabilistic boolean output (True or False) paired with an explicit confidence score. score : A bounded numeric rating (typically 0–100) indicating intensity, risk, or priority. 2. Comparison: Generative LLMs vs. Decision Models vs. Classical ML Dimension Generative LLMs (e.g. GPT-4o, Claude) Decision Models (TypeSafe AI Jev) Classical ML (e.g. Scikit / XGBoost) Output Type Autoregressive text stream Strictly typed ( choice , noul , score ) Fixed class label / float probability P95 Latency 1,500ms – 5,000ms 80ms – 180ms 5ms – 20ms Schema Reliability Prone to formatting hallucination 100% deterministic type safety 100% deterministic Zero-Shot Generalization High High (understands complex semantic context) Low (requires custom training & feature engineering) Input Flexibility Text, multimodal images Text, clean DOM trees, JSON state Pre-engineered feature vectors Cost Profile High ($2.50 – $15.00 / 1M tokens) Low (fractions of a cent per batch) Lowest (self-hosted compute) 3. Six Real-World Architecture Patterns flowchart TD A [Incoming Request / Event] --> B {Jev Decision Gate} B --> |Flagged: Security Violation| C [Drop & Alert SecOps] B --> |Simple FAQ / Low Urgency| D [Route to Fast SLM / Auto-Reply] B --> |High Complexity / Reasoning| E [Route to Claude 3.7 / o3] B --> |High Risk / Account Blocker| F [Queue for Human Tier 1 Support] 1. Cost & Model Tier Routing Sending every user prompt to an expensive reasoning model (e.g., OpenAI o3 or Claude Opus) burns capital unnecessarily. Jev acts as an ingress router: It scores prompt complexity ( score ) and selects the appropriate model tier ( choice : ["slm", "general_llm", "reasoning_model"] ). 70% of mundane queries resolve through sub-cent SLMs without human-perceptible latency. 2. Inline Agent Guardrails & Jailbreak Detection Running a complete LLM before every tool call doubles execution time. A Jev noul question placed directly in front of Python/Bash/SQL tool executors checks: "Does this tool call attempt command injection, directory traversal, or…

title: Enterprise Claude Code on AWS Bedrock: Multi-User SSO, Governance, and AI Admin Playbook
description: A complete engineering guide to deploying Anthropic's Claude Code across enterprise developer teams using AWS Bedrock, IAM Identity Center SSO, Bedrock Guardrails, and audit-ready governance.
text: As engineering teams adopt Claude Code (Anthropic's agentic command-line tool), platform engineers and security administrators face a familiar friction: developer agility vs. enterprise compliance. In a hobby project, developers export static API keys ( ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-... ) into local .env files. In an enterprise organization, hardcoded API keys are an existential security risk—they cannot be attributed to human identities, they lack automated revocation, and they bypass corporate DLP, egress policies, and auditing controls. The production-grade solution is to run Claude Code over Amazon Bedrock , underpinned by AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO) , temporary STS credential vending, and Bedrock Guardrails . In this guide, we walk through the end-to-end architecture: provisioning multi-user SSO, configuration multiplexing on local machines, auditing AI invocations, and defending your posture during rigorous security and compliance audits. 1. The Core Architecture: Federated SSO & Credential Vending Instead of long-lived API tokens, every developer request should be authenticated through your central Identity Provider (Okta, Google Workspace, Azure AD, or AWS IAM Identity Center) and bound to short-lived AWS STS credentials. sequenceDiagram autonumber actor Dev as Developer Machine (Claude Code) participant SSO as AWS IAM Identity Center (SSO / IdP) participant STS as AWS Security Token Service (STS) participant Bedrock as Amazon Bedrock (Claude 3.7 / 3.5 Sonnet) participant Guardrail as Bedrock Guardrail (PII Masking & Topics) participant Logs as S3 Invocation Bucket & CloudTrail Dev ->> SSO : aws sso login (Web browser OAuth) SSO ->> STS : AssumeRoleWithSSO (Team Permission Set) STS -->> Dev : Return short-lived session token (e.g. 8h expiry) Dev ->> Bedrock : Execute Claude Code command (CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1) Bedrock ->> Guardrail : Inspect prompt (PII check, prompt-injection filter) alt Policy Violation Guardrail -->> Dev : Blocked / Denied by organization policy else Clean Prompt Guardrail ->> Bedrock : Forward payload to model Bedrock ->> Logs : Stream user prompt, completion, & token metadata to S3 Bedrock -->> Dev : Stream code completion to CLI end Architectural Concepts in Play Federated Single Sign-On (SSO): Developers do not have IAM user accounts or passwords. They log in with their corporate identity. Temporary Credential Vending: Running aws sso login fetches short-lived tokens. If a laptop is stolen, credentials expire automatically without manual key rotation. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC): Developers belong to groups (e.g., Platform-Engineers , Backend-Devs ) mapped to permission sets granting bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream . Client-Side Sandbox Multiplexing: Using CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR to maintain strict isolation between work accounts and personal environments on a single machine. 2. Step-by-Step Implementation Phase 1: AWS Administrator Setup First, activate Bedrock model access and configure least-privilege IAM policies. 1. Enable Anthropic Models In the Amazon Bedrock Console , navigate to Model catalog , request access to the desired models (e.g., Anthropic Claude 3.7 Sonnet or Claude 3.5 Sonnet ), and submit the standard use-case form. 2. Create the IAM Permission Set In IAM Identity Center , create a permission set named ClaudeCodeDeveloperAccess with the following inline policy: { "Version" : "2012-10-17" , "Statement" : [ { "Sid" : "BedrockModelInvocation" , "Effect" : "Allow" , "Action" : [ "bedrock:InvokeModel" , "bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream" ] , "Resource" : [ "arn:aws:bedrock:*::foundation-model/anthropic.claude-*" ] } , { "Sid" : "BedrockEnforceGuardrails" , "Effect" : "Allow" , "Action" : [ "bedrock:ApplyGuardrail" ] , "Resource" : "arn:aws:bedrock:*:*:guardrail/*" } ] } Assign this permission set to your developer groups in your target AWS account. title: From SQLite to Mem0: Architecting Production Memory & Persistence for LangGraph Agents
description: A deep architectural guide on scaling LangGraph memory from local SQLite checkpointers to production PostgreSQL pooling, Redis session caching, and semantic agent memory layers like Mem0.
text: When building stateful AI agents with LangGraph , the path from prototype to production is paved with memory decisions. In official quickstarts, you often see SqliteSaver used as a lightweight checkpointer: you point it at a local .db file, and suddenly your agent remembers conversations across multiple turns. It feels effortless—until you deploy it to multi-user, multi-instance production environments. In this deep dive, we explore how memory actually works in LangGraph, why SQLite hits a hard wall in production, and how modern agentic architectures combine PostgreSQL connection pooling , Redis caching , and intelligent semantic memory layers like Mem0 to support high-concurrency, personalized agent workflows. 1. LangGraph Memory Anatomy: Checkpointers vs. Stores LangGraph bifurcates agent memory into two distinct abstractions: ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ LangGraph Memory │ ├───────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────┤ │ Short-Term / Thread │ Long-Term / Cross- │ │ (Checkpointers) │ Thread (Stores) │ │ │ │ │ • State checkpointing │ • User profiles & traits │ │ • Per-session trajectory │ • Durable facts & habits │ │ • Time-travel & branching │ • Cross-session memories │ │ • Rollbacks & human-loop │ • Semantic search recall │ └───────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┘ Short-Term Thread Memory (Checkpointers): Implemented via BaseCheckpointSaver (e.g., MemorySaver , SqliteSaver , PostgresSaver ). Saves graph state snapshots after each node executes. Allows resuming interrupted flows, human-in-the-loop approvals, and rollbacks. Scoped strictly to a thread_id . Long-Term Cross-Thread Memory (Stores): Implemented via the BaseStore interface. Preserves knowledge across different threads and interaction sessions for a given user or organization. Houses user preferences, extracted facts, and historical patterns. 2. The SQLite Wall in Production SqliteSaver is an embedded database engine running directly in your application process: from langgraph . checkpoint . sqlite import SqliteSaver # Great for local development: memory = SqliteSaver . from_conn_string ( "checkpoints.db" ) graph = builder . compile ( checkpointer = memory ) While great for local CLI testing, SQLite runs into major architectural limitations when deployed to cloud environments: The Single-Writer Concurrency Bottleneck SQLite uses database-level locks for writes. When multiple concurrent users interact with your agent, simultaneous graph state commits queue up. Under moderate traffic spikes, requests quickly fail with sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked or experience extreme latency tail-ends. Ephemeral Containers & Distributed Instances Modern cloud deployments run on Kubernetes, ECS, or serverless containers with multiple horizontal replicas. A local SQLite file lives on an ephemeral container volume: Multiple replicas cannot safely share a single SQLite file across network mounts (NFS/EFS) without risking write corruption and lock contention. When an auto-scaling group spins down a container, all local checkpoint history is destroyed. Lack of Enterprise HA & Point-in-Time Recovery Production workloads require automated failover, streaming replication, read replicas, and point-in-time recovery (PITR)—capabilities that server-based relational engines deliver out of the box. 3. Scaling Checkpointers: PostgreSQL & Connection Pooling The primary production replacement for short-term graph checkpointing is PostgreSQL , using langgraph-checkpoint-postgres with asynchronous connection pooling. from langgraph . checkpoint . postgres . aio import AsyncPostgresSaver from psycopg_pool import AsyncConnectionPool DB_URI = "postgresql://user:pass@ep-db.cloud.internal:5432/agent_db" async def initialize_agent_graph ( ) : # Maintain a robust connection pool across agent executions async with AsyncConnectionPool ( conninfo = DB_URI , max_size = 20 ) as pool : checkpointer = AsyncPostg…

title: LangChain vs LangGraph: Architecting Stateful Multi-Agent Systems
description: A deep dive into the architectural differences between LangChain and LangGraph, including state management, cycles, and multi-agent coordination.
text: The landscape of building LLM-powered applications is evolving rapidly. We've moved from simple prompt engineering to complex "chains," and now we're entering the era of truly agentic, multi-agent systems. When you're architecting these systems, the choice between LangChain and LangGraph is critical. While they share a lineage, their architectural foundations are built for fundamentally different use cases. The Architectural Divide: Linear vs. Cyclic At its core, the difference is one of topology: Linear Chains vs. Cyclic Graphs. Feature LangChain (Chains) LangGraph (Graphs) Topology Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) Cyclic Graph Flow Linear / Sequential Looping / Iterative State Implicit / Append-only Explicit / Schema-based Cycles Not natively supported First-class citizen Persistence Basic memory buffers Checkpointing / Time Travel LangChain: The Linear Evolution LangChain is built around the concept of a DAG. You define a sequence of steps—a "chain"—where data flows from one component to the next in a predetermined path. It’s excellent for straightforward transformations and simple RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation). LangGraph: The Agentic Revolution LangGraph is designed for stateful, cyclic workflows . Instead of a fixed sequence, you define a graph where Nodes represent actions (LLM calls, tools) and Edges define transitions. Control Flow & Decision Making Transitions in LangGraph aren't just direct; you use Conditional Edges (routers) to make real-time decisions. For example, a router node can analyze an LLM's output and decide whether to call a tool or move to a final response node. Advanced State Management One of the most significant upgrades in LangGraph is how it treats state. Explicit State Schemas In LangGraph, you define a State object (using TypedDict or Pydantic ). This provides a single source of truth that is passed between every node in the graph. ReducedValue : Allows you to define custom state reducers (e.g., merging a list of messages instead of overwriting). UntrackedValue : Useful for transient data that needs to be accessible within a node but shouldn't be persisted in the graph's history. Reliability: Persistence & Human-in-the-Loop Checkpoints and Time Travel LangGraph includes built-in Persistence . Every step of the graph is checkpointed. If a system crashes, you can resume exactly where you left off. This also enables Time Travel , allowing you to "rewind" to a previous state, inspect what the agent was thinking, and even branch into a new execution path. Interrupts For sensitive actions (like executing a shell command or making a transaction), LangGraph supports Interrupts . You can pause the graph, wait for a human to approve the action, and then resume. Multi-Agent Architecture Patterns When scaling to multiple agents, LangGraph supports three primary patterns: Supervisor: A central manager agent delegates tasks to specialized workers. Collaborative: Agents share a common state and pass control back and forth directly. Swarm: A decentralized collection of agents that coordinate through shared memory and triggers. Practical Example: The Self-Correction Loop A classic use case for LangGraph is a Self-Correction Loop : Agent Node : Generates code. Test Node : Executes the code and runs unit tests. Conditional Edge : If tests pass, move to End . If they fail, route back to the Agent Node with the error log for a fix. Security & Stability (March 2026 Update) Stability is as important as architecture. As of March 2026, several critical security advisories have been released concerning AI framework vulnerabilities: CVE-2026-34070 : Path Traversal in legacy prompt loading. CVE-2025-68664 : Serialization injection in dumps() and load() . CVE-2025-67644 : Unsafe deserialization of LLM-influenced metadata. To mitigate these, ensure your systems are running langchain-core (1.2.22+) and langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite (3.0.1+) . These versions deprecate unsafe legacy fun…

title: Multi-Turn Conversation with LLM
description: A detailed guide on structuring multi-turn conversations with Large Language Models for optimal results, focusing on topic management and framework design.
text: Multi-Turn Conversation with LLM In this post, we will discuss various methods available for handling multi-turn conversations with Large Language Models (LLMs). With the release of early systems like "Launch Pad," we achieved some level of multi-turn conversation. However, a key question remains: How should the system act and interact? Currently, most LLM-based experiences act by collecting client information and acknowledging the user with specific responses. Guardrails often prevent the LLM from going off-topic, sticking rigidly to engineered prompts. However, there are limitations: Time limits : Often limited to 2 minutes; increasing this can make the LLM go "off the rails." Task/Goal support : Current implementations often lack clear task or goal handling. Topic handling : There's often no explicit mechanism for topic switching or management. Let's explore ways to tackle these limitations and achieve longer, more coherent conversations using Dialog Management . LLM-Based Agent Framework One promising approach is a specialized Large Language Model (LLM) tailored for Goal-Oriented Dialogue (GOD) , which is particularly effective in complex diagnostic scenarios like medical or legal consultations. Unlike general chatbots, a specialized system can proactively guide users toward specific outcomes by managing dialogue topics and maintaining state. The Framework The framework consists of four main components: Thinking Topic Development Maintaining Topic Stack Enriching Topic Generating Response 1. Thinking Topic Development When starting a conversation, the first step is picking a topic. The system analyzes the user's query and decides the main topic for the current round of dialogue. How it works: Receives user query. Analyzes previous dialogue context to identify user interest. Influences conversation direction for a relevant, engaging response. 2. Maintaining Topic Stack Imagine juggling several conversation threads—talking about a project, planning a meetup, and discussing a movie. Maintaining a "stack" allows the system to track these threads and switch between them without losing context. How it works: Maintains a "stack" of topics discussed. Adds new topics to the top; removes resolved or irrelevant ones. Manages the flow, ensuring all points are addressed smoothly. 3. Enriching Topic This adds details to make the conversation more engaging. For example, if discussing soccer, enrichment might include player stats or notable moments. How it works: Looks for ways to add relevant details to a chosen topic. Pulls in background info, related topics, or deeper insights. Keeps the user engaged with comprehensive context. 4. Generating Response The final step is forming the reply based on the topic, enriched information, and context. How it works: Combines the current topic, enriched info, and history. Uses rules and models to advance the conversation toward user goals. Considers user preferences and tone for a natural feel. Example: Collect Basic User Information Task Definition { "task_name" : "Collect Basic User Information" , "overview" : "Collecting essential personal and contact information from a user to create or update their profile." , "goal" : "Accurately collect and record all necessary user information" , "checklist" : [ "Ask for user's full name" , "Request date of birth for eligibility" , "Inquire about email address" , "Collect phone number for urgent queries" , "Ask for home address" , "Confirm data consent" , "Summarize info for verification" , "Provide confirmation number" ] } Sample Chat History User: Collect Basic User Information Virtual Assistant: Thank you for reaching out. May I have your full name, please? User: My full name is Rohit Marathe Virtual Assistant: Thank you, Rohit. May I also ask for your date of birth for eligibility verification? User: Yeah sure, I was born on 25 Aug 1995 Virtual Assistant: Thank you. May I have your email address for communication? …

title: Hello World — Why I'm Starting This Blog
description: An introduction to who I am, what I do as an AI Systems Engineer, and what you can expect from this blog.
text: If you're reading this, welcome! I'm Rohit — an AI Systems Engineer currently building intelligent systems at Rocket Mortgage in Atlanta. I've spent the last 6+ years working at the intersection of software engineering and artificial intelligence, from building conversational AI bots at Kore.ai to architecting multi-agent systems that handle millions of requests in production. Why a blog? I've learned so much from engineers who share their knowledge openly — blog posts that saved me hours of debugging, architecture write-ups that shaped how I think about systems, and tutorials that helped me pick up new tools. It's time I give back. This blog is where I'll write about: Building AI systems in production — not just the theory, but the messy reality of deploying LLMs at scale Multi-agent orchestration — patterns, pitfalls, and what actually works when you need multiple AI agents to collaborate Cloud engineering — AWS, Kubernetes, and the infrastructure that makes AI systems reliable Lessons from the field — things I wish I knew earlier, debugging war stories, and career reflections What I won't do I'm not going to write generic "What is AI?" explainers. There are plenty of those. Instead, I'll share the things I've learned by actually building and operating these systems — the decisions, trade-offs, and hard-won insights that come from production experience. Let's connect If any of this resonates with you, I'd love to connect. Find me on GitHub or LinkedIn , or just keep reading. Let's build something cool. 🚀

title: Multi-Agent Orchestration — Patterns That Actually Work
description: Practical patterns for building multi-agent AI systems in production, from routing strategies to failover architecture.
text: After spending the past year building multi-agent systems at Rocket Mortgage, I've learned that the gap between a demo and production is enormous. Here are the patterns that actually survived contact with real traffic. The Problem A single LLM prompt can answer simple questions. But when you need an AI system to handle mortgage calculations, search property databases, analyze banker performance, and diagnose system alerts — you need specialization. That's where multi-agent orchestration comes in: instead of one monolithic prompt, you build a system of specialized agents that collaborate. Pattern 1: Router-Based Orchestration The simplest pattern that works. A central router agent classifies incoming requests and delegates to the appropriate specialist. class OrchestratorRouter : def __init__ ( self , agents : dict [ str , Agent ] ) : self . agents = agents self . classifier = ClassifierAgent ( ) async def handle ( self , request : UserRequest ) - > Response : intent = await self . classifier . classify ( request ) agent = self . agents [ intent ] return await agent . execute ( request ) When to use it: When your agents have clearly distinct domains and requests rarely need multiple agents. The catch: Classification accuracy is everything. A misrouted request gives the user a completely wrong answer with full confidence. We found that adding a confidence threshold and falling back to a general agent for low-confidence classifications cut our error rate by 20%. Pattern 2: Multi-LLM Failover Production systems can't go down. We built a failover architecture that routes between Claude and GPT-4 based on availability and rate limits. class MultiLLMClient : def __init__ ( self , providers : list [ LLMProvider ] ) : self . providers = providers # ordered by preference async def complete ( self , prompt : str ) - > str : for provider in self . providers : if provider . is_available ( ) : try : return await provider . complete ( prompt ) except RateLimitError : provider . mark_limited ( ) continue raise AllProvidersExhaustedError ( ) The key insight: rate-limiting guardrails must be proactive, not reactive. By the time you get a 429 response, you've already wasted latency. We track token consumption in real-time and start routing to the backup provider before hitting the limit. Pattern 3: Self-Healing Agents This is the one I'm most proud of. We built an agent that monitors system alerts, diagnoses root causes using RAG over our runbooks, and executes remediation scripts autonomously. The architecture: Alert ingestion — System alert comes in via webhook Context retrieval — RAG searches our knowledge base of past incidents and runbooks Diagnosis — LLM analyzes the alert + retrieved context to identify root cause Action planning — Agent proposes remediation steps using function calling Execution — Approved actions are executed via MCP server integration The critical guardrail: never auto-execute destructive actions. Our agent can restart services and clear caches autonomously, but anything involving data modification requires human approval. What I'd Do Differently If I were starting over, I'd invest more in observability from day one . We eventually built an LLM-as-a-Judge pipeline with Langfuse that continuously evaluates agent responses, but we should have had that from the start. When you have multiple agents in a pipeline, debugging "why did the system give a wrong answer?" becomes a multi-step investigation. Good tracing makes this 10x easier. Key Takeaways Start simple — Router-based orchestration handles 80% of use cases Build for failure — Multi-LLM failover is not optional in production Observe everything — You can't improve what you can't measure Guardrails are features — The best agent is one that knows when not to act I'll dive deeper into each of these patterns in future posts. If you're building something similar, I'd love to hear about your approach — reach out on LinkedIn .

title: Essential Design Patterns Every Engineer Should Know
description: A practical guide to the most important software design patterns — Factory, Observer, Strategy, and Singleton — with real-world examples and when to use each.
text: Design patterns are battle-tested solutions to recurring problems in software design. You don't need to memorize all 23 Gang of Four patterns — but knowing the essential ones will make you a significantly better engineer. Here are the patterns I use most in production systems, with practical examples that go beyond textbook definitions. 1. Factory Pattern — "Don't new Things Directly" The Factory pattern delegates object creation to a separate method or class, so your code doesn't need to know the exact class it's creating. Why It Matters Imagine you're building an AI system that needs to support multiple LLM providers — Claude, GPT-4, and Gemini. Without a factory, every place you create a provider is tightly coupled: # ❌ Bad — tightly coupled if provider_name == "claude" : client = ClaudeClient ( api_key = key , model = "claude-3" ) elif provider_name == "gpt4" : client = OpenAIClient ( api_key = key , model = "gpt-4" ) elif provider_name == "gemini" : client = GeminiClient ( api_key = key , model = "gemini-pro" ) With a factory, creation logic lives in one place: # ✅ Good — Factory pattern class LLMFactory : _providers = { "claude" : ClaudeClient , "gpt4" : OpenAIClient , "gemini" : GeminiClient , } @classmethod def create ( cls , provider : str , ** kwargs ) - > LLMClient : if provider not in cls . _providers : raise ValueError ( f"Unknown provider: { provider } " ) return cls . _providers [ provider ] ( ** kwargs ) # Usage — clean and extensible client = LLMFactory . create ( "claude" , api_key = key , model = "claude-3" ) When to Use It You need to create objects without specifying their exact class You want to centralize complex creation logic You need to swap implementations easily (testing, A/B experiments) 2. Observer Pattern — "Notify Everyone Who Cares" The Observer pattern lets objects subscribe to events and get notified when something changes — without the publisher knowing who's listening. Real-World Example In a monitoring system, when a deployment completes, multiple systems need to react: class EventBus : def __init__ ( self ) : self . _subscribers : dict [ str , list [ Callable ] ] = { } def subscribe ( self , event : str , callback : Callable ) : self . _subscribers . setdefault ( event , [ ] ) . append ( callback ) def publish ( self , event : str , data : dict ) : for callback in self . _subscribers . get ( event , [ ] ) : callback ( data ) # Set up observers bus = EventBus ( ) bus . subscribe ( "deploy.complete" , send_slack_notification ) bus . subscribe ( "deploy.complete" , update_dashboard ) bus . subscribe ( "deploy.complete" , run_smoke_tests ) bus . subscribe ( "deploy.failed" , page_oncall_engineer ) # Publisher doesn't know or care who's listening bus . publish ( "deploy.complete" , { "service" : "api" , "version" : "2.1.0" } ) When to Use It Multiple components need to react to the same event You want loose coupling between event producers and consumers Building notification systems, event-driven architectures, or UI state management 3. Strategy Pattern — "Swap Algorithms at Runtime" The Strategy pattern lets you define a family of algorithms, put each in its own class, and make them interchangeable. Real-World Example Different documents need different chunking strategies for a RAG pipeline: from abc import ABC , abstractmethod class ChunkingStrategy ( ABC ) : @abstractmethod def chunk ( self , text : str ) - > list [ str ] : pass class FixedSizeChunking ( ChunkingStrategy ) : def __init__ ( self , size : int = 512 , overlap : int = 50 ) : self . size = size self . overlap = overlap def chunk ( self , text : str ) - > list [ str ] : chunks = [ ] for i in range ( 0 , len ( text ) , self . size - self . overlap ) : chunks . append ( text [ i : i + self . size ] ) return chunks class SemanticChunking ( ChunkingStrategy ) : def chunk ( self , text : str ) - > list [ str ] : # Split on paragraph boundaries for semantic coherence return [ p . strip ( ) for p in text . …

title: System Design 101 — Building Blocks of Scalable Systems
description: A beginner-friendly guide to the fundamental building blocks of system design: load balancers, caching, databases, message queues, and CDNs.
text: System design interviews can feel overwhelming, but every complex system is built from the same fundamental components. Once you understand these building blocks, you can reason about any architecture. This post covers the core components you'll see in every system design — with practical explanations of why each exists and when to use it. The Big Picture Before diving into individual components, here's how they fit together in a typical web-scale system: Every request flows through this chain. Let me break down each component. 1. Load Balancer — "Distribute the Traffic" A load balancer sits in front of your servers and distributes incoming requests across multiple instances. It's the reason Netflix doesn't crash when 100 million people hit play at 8 PM. How It Works Client Request ↓ ┌─────────────────┐ │ Load Balancer │ └─────────────────┘ ↓ ↓ ↓ Server1 Server2 Server3 Common Algorithms Algorithm How It Works Best For Round Robin Requests rotate through servers in order Equal-capacity servers Least Connections Sends to the server with fewest active connections Varying request complexity IP Hash Same client IP always goes to same server Session persistence Weighted More traffic to beefier servers Mixed hardware Key Insight Load balancers also handle health checks — they stop sending traffic to unhealthy servers automatically. This is how you achieve high availability without manual intervention. # Simplified health check logic class LoadBalancer : def __init__ ( self , servers : list [ Server ] ) : self . servers = servers def get_healthy_server ( self ) - > Server : healthy = [ s for s in self . servers if s . health_check ( ) ] return min ( healthy , key = lambda s : s . active_connections ) 2. Caching — "Don't Compute the Same Thing Twice" Caching stores frequently accessed data in fast storage (usually memory) to avoid hitting slower databases or APIs repeatedly. Cache Tiers Request → L1 (In-Memory, ~1ms) → L2 (Redis, ~5ms) → Database (~50ms) Cache Strategies Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) — The most common pattern: async def get_user ( user_id : str ) - > User : # 1. Check cache first cached = await redis . get ( f"user: { user_id } " ) if cached : return User . from_json ( cached ) # 2. Cache miss — fetch from database user = await db . query ( "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?" , user_id ) # 3. Store in cache for next time (expire in 5 minutes) await redis . set ( f"user: { user_id } " , user . to_json ( ) , ex = 300 ) return user Write-Through — Write to cache and database simultaneously: async def update_user ( user_id : str , data : dict ) : # Write to both — cache is always fresh await db . update ( "users" , user_id , data ) await redis . set ( f"user: { user_id } " , json . dumps ( data ) , ex = 300 ) Cache Invalidation "There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things." — Phil Karlton Common invalidation strategies: Strategy Mechanism Trade-off TTL (Time-to-Live) Expires after N seconds Simple but stale reads possible Event-based Invalidate on write events Fresh data but more complex Version-based Key includes version number Precise but coordination needed 3. Database — "Where the Truth Lives" SQL vs NoSQL — The Real Decision Framework Don't pick your database based on hype. Pick it based on your access patterns: Choose SQL When Choose NoSQL When Data has relationships (joins) Data is denormalized/nested You need ACID transactions You need horizontal scaling Schema is well-defined Schema evolves rapidly Complex queries needed Simple key-value lookups Database Scaling Patterns Read Replicas — Scale reads by copying data to replica databases: Writes → Primary DB Reads → Replica 1, Replica 2, Replica 3 This is the first scaling move most systems make.
